title: Choose, then trust
hookLine: think long before making a friend, then trust them wholly
carry: speak as boldly with them as with yourself

lines: MY FRIEND. BUT DON'T TELL HIM.
cards: Lucilius has sent Seneca some letters, carried by a man he calls his friend. And in the same note he adds: but please don't discuss my affairs with him. You can almost hear Seneca put the letter down and raise an eyebrow.

A friend you can't talk in front of? It's a small slip, and an easy one: calling someone a friend after two good dinners, then staying careful around them for years. Seneca's third letter turns that slip inside out.

teach.h: A FRIEND, OR NOT A FRIEND.
teach.b: Lucilius, Seneca says, is using the word friend loosely, the way people greet anyone as dear sir. Either this man is a real friend or he isn't. If he is, trust him.
If he isn't, don't call him one. Then the rule. Think a long time about whether someone should be admitted to your friendship.
Once you've decided, welcome them with your whole heart, and speak as boldly with them as with yourself. Judge before the friendship; trust after it.
Some people get this backwards, Seneca says, citing the philosopher Theophrastus: they love first and judge later, and then can't decide whether to keep loving.
There are two mistakes. Some people tell everything to anyone who'll listen, unloading secrets into any ear they meet. Others won't confide even in those closest to them, and lock away every thought.
Both are faults: one trusts everyone, the other no one. The care in choosing is what makes the trust possible.

teach.h: CARE AT THE GATE, PEACE INSIDE.
teach.b: If you take a long time over the gate, you don't have to stand guard inside the house. That doesn't mean a friend can never let you down. It means that once you've chosen, you stop treating your friend like a suspect.
The looking comes first, so the trust can be whole.

how: Following Seneca, some people are slow and careful about whom they call a close friend, and then speak openly with those they've chosen.

o: decide quickly, and trust a new friend at once
pick friends by how much you enjoy their company
judge with care before calling someone a friend

games.q: choose, then trust — tap the pairs.

s: Seneca says a wise person should never fully trust anyone
once you've chosen a friend, he says, trust them with your whole heart.
Seneca cites Theophrastus on judging before loving
he says some love first and judge after, against Theophrastus' advice.
Lucilius had called a man his friend but asked Seneca not to talk business with him
that slip is how the third letter begins.

games.q: you're Seneca. Lucilius calls a man his friend, then asks you not to discuss his affairs in front of him. what do you write back?
o: either he's a friend and you trust him, or he isn't, so don't call him one.
say nothing; it's not your business.
games.why: Seneca says the word friend is being used loosely: judge carefully first, and then, if he's a friend, trust him wholly.

practice: Bring to mind one person you've already chosen, someone who has shown you over time who they are, and notice anything you've been holding back from them out of habit: a worry, a hope, a thank you.
You don't have to say it now; just picture telling them plainly, the way you'd say it to yourself, and breathe with the trust instead of the guard.

wordCard.voice: Choose. Seneca's third letter: think long before you call someone a friend; once you have, trust them as you trust yourself. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: after friendship, trust; before friendship, judge. From Seneca's third letter.

carryVoice: Your line: speak as boldly with them as with yourself. Judge before the friendship; trust after it. Day four hundred thirty-five.
